title: NUMA & PCIe KV-shard microbench: MoE gating impact on long-context Llama/Mistral/Qwen
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note from a set of microbench experiments exploring how KV-cache sharding across NUMA nodes and across PCIe-connected devices affects MoE routing/gating latency and throughput for long-context workloads (16k–32k). We compare behavior on representative model families (Llama-like dense, Mistral mix, Qwen-style attention layout) while varying gating policy (top-1, top-2) and expert placement (local vs spread).

Motivation / problem statement:
- In Dedicated/Private deployments we sometimes run MoE models with long contexts (>=16k).
- The serving runtime shards KV across accelerators and occasionally across NUMA/PCIe boundaries for memory reasons (activation capacity).
- Anecdotal regressions: p99 jumps when gate fanout increases or when requests touch cross-socket memory. We need systematic microbench data and actionable mitigations.

Hardware baseline (test rigs):
- Node A: 2x AMD EPYC 7742 (64C), 8x A100 80GB, NVLink mesh inside each NVSwitch group. Linux 5.15, CUDA 11.8.
- Node B: 2x Intel Xeon Platinum, 4x A40 (PCIe x16 interleaved), general PCIe fabric (no NVLink between GPUs).
- Multi-node test: Node A + Node B connected via PCIe/IB where noted.

Workloads and models:
- LL-DENSE: Llama-13B style dense transformer, 32k context synthetic tokens (random, deterministic prefix).
- MRL-MIX: Mistral-like 7B mixture-of-experts variant used for internal repro (64 experts), long-window 16k/32k.
- QWEN-ATT: Qwen-7B-ish with wider attention layout, long sequences 16k.
- All runs use runtime v3.11 benchmark harness (internal script: bench/kv_shard_micro.sh).

Gating variants tested:
- top-1 deterministic (softmax gating -> top1 argmax)
- top-2 balanced (pair of experts with load-balancing temperature)
- probabilistic sampling (for completeness)

Experiment matrix (summary):
- Placement: experts co-located (local-group) vs spread-even (round-robin across GPUs) vs NUMA-aware (experts packed by socket)
- Fabric: NVLink (intra-node NVSwitch), PCIe-only (Node B), cross-node (spread across NodeA+NodeB)
- KV distribution: per-GPU full-KV vs split-shard (each GPU holds slice of KV for all tokens)
- Batch profiles: single-stream 1 request / burst 8 concurrent streams / steady-state 64 small streams

Commands & instrumentation (how to reproduce):
- bench harness: bench/kv_shard_micro.sh --model {LL-DENSE|MRL-MIX|QWEN-ATT} --context 32000 --gating {top1|top2|sample} --placement {local|spread|numa} --fabric {nvlink|pcie|cross}
- profiling: nsys profile --sample=none --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --output=run1
- CPU perf: perf record -a -g -F 99 -- /usr/bin/bench-driver
- memory map: pmap -x <pid> and numactl --hardware for affinity verification

Key raw observations (numbers are median of 5 runs; tokens/sec and p99 in ms):
- Baseline dense single-GPU (NVLink, no sharding): LL-DENSE 32k: throughput 840 tok/s, p99 14ms.
- MRl-MIX top1, experts co-located, NVLink: throughput 540 tok/s, p99 28ms.
- MRL-MIX top2, experts spread-even over PCIe-only node: throughput 310 tok/s, p99 72ms (high jitter).
- QWEN-ATT across NodeA+NodeB (cross-node PCIe shuffle for gate fanout): throughput 260 tok/s, p99 98ms; observed frequent GPU-to-GPU PCIe transfers during gating window.
- NUMA mismatch (experts assigned across sockets but GPUs attached to single socket): observed 18–35% extra latency vs socket-local placement even when GPUs were NVLinked within a socket group.

Detailed traces insights:
- When gating fanout >1 and spread-even placement, we see two phases: (1) gating decision compute (~1–2 ms) then (2) expert activation fetch/kv-merge where the majority of additional latency appears. The second phase includes PCIe DMA or NVLink peer-to-peer transfers depending on fabric.
- Cross-socket CPU memory touches: for shard layouts where CPU managed memory pages (UVM/emulated) are accessed by GPUs on the other socket, we see kernel-level page migration and CPU interruptions; perf shows <pgfault> spikes synchronized with p99 spikes.
- On PCIe-only rigs, nsys shows memcpy H2D/D2H roundtrips during expert shuffle. NVLink rigs show fewer explicit copies but higher NVSwitch internal contention for multi-expert workloads.

Hypotheses (ordered by confidence):
1) Fanout-induced shuffle cost dominates p99 when experts are spread across different PCIe/NVLink domains. The cost is proportional to number of distinct transfer domains touched per request.
2) NUMA-crossing CPU page faults and kernel migrations amplify latency when KV shards are backed by CPU memory (UVM) or when runtime pins pages suboptimally.
3) Small-batch steady-state with many concurrent streams exposes serialization points in the expert-resolver (mutexes) leading to tail amplification; this is aggravated when combined with cross-device DMA.
4) Qwen-like attention layouts with larger per-layer activation expand the per-expert data volume and thus multiply the shuffle cost (bandwidth-bound).

Actionable mitigations tested and their effect:
- Expert co-location by socket (pack experts that are likely to be used together onto same NVLink domain): reduced p99 by up to 40% in top-2 runs.
- Prefetch + local-cache: added a tiny per-request prefetch to pull likely-expert KV into local GPU memory before gating completion; reduced p99 jitter but added steady-state CPU overhead. Overall p99 improvement 15–25%.
- Gating temperature tuning (bias toward top1): trading a small hit in model perplexity reduced average fanout and improved latency by ~20% for MRl-MIX. Suggest exposing this knob at serving policy level.
- NUMA-aware mmap/pinning in runtime: binding allocation and mapping to the CPU socket local to the GPUs reduced pagefaults and lowered p99 by 18% in cross-socket experiments.
- Batch coalescing: when many small concurrent streams exist, grouping them to leverage fewer large transfers lowered PCIe overhead; throughput up but increased average latency slightly — good for throughput-first SLAs.

Risks / quality trade-offs:
- Prefetching increases upstream CPU utilization and may impact other tenants on shared nodes. Should gate per-tenant or per-priority.
- Co-locating experts can create hot-expert hotspots; must combine with load-aware replication or fallback to balanced placement on overload.
- Gating bias could change model outputs for edge-case tasks. Need offline evals (eval prompt suites) and rollout gating.

Suggested short-term changes for runtime (low effort -> high impact):
1) Add a "placement policy" flag: numa-local / nvlink-aware / spread. Default to nvlink-aware for dedicated NVSwitch nodes. (PR idea: runtime/config/placement_policy)
2) Add simple prefetch hook in gate pipeline: issue async memcpy of KV for candidate experts while gating compute finishes. (Careful with memory pressure.)
3) Improve mmap/pin logic: on allocation, pin pages to socket local with fallback. (Small kernel/OS caveat tests on Ubuntu 20.04 and 22.04 required.)

Longer-term research agenda:
- Dynamic expert replication: replicate hot experts onto multiple NVLink domains and add a locality-aware resolver at routing time.
- Topology-aware routing ML: train a small routing cost model predicting end-to-end latency per-gating decision that includes placement cost; use for routing decisions at request time.
- Hardware-accelerated shuffle: evaluate use of RDMA for cross-node expert fetches (requires support from on-prem infra).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Re-run popular customer MoE workloads (JIRA-ENG-1427) with placement_policy nvlink-aware to measure end-to-end customer p99 impact.
- Quantify model quality vs gating-bias tradeoff on eval suite (eval/kv_gating_bias.ipynb).
- Trace mutex contention in expert-resolver to determine if lock-free structures or per-expert queues reduce tail.

Appendix: quick reproduction notes & files
- bench/kv_shard_micro.sh (internal repro)
- nsys traces: traces/run_2025_11_03_top2_spread.nsys (linked in internal bucket)
- Partial perf sample: perf_samples/top2_spread_pid1234.txt
- Relevant PRs: runtime/pinning and runtime/placement-policy (see linked_artifacts)

Author notes (freeform):
- This doc is intentionally experimental and fairly noisy. The top actionable win we've seen so far is "pack experts by NVLink domain" + "NUMA-aware pinning". Prefetch helps but must be tuned.
- The variance across model families is non-linear: Qwen-like attention pumps up the data transfer size sufficiently that even NVLink runs start to look bandwidth-bound instead of latency-bound. Keep an eye on bytes-per-token estimates when onboarding new archs.

Next steps (owners):
- (Aisha) implement placement_policy flag + basic socket packing in a branch; run regression on customer workload (due 2025-11-17).
- (Marco) validate mmap/pin heuristics on NodeB (PCIe-only) and confirm no regressions on other kernels (due 2025-11-12).
- (Emily) run gating-bias offline evals and produce a small report (due 2025-11-20).
